newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Shelling after Congo's Lissouba returns home.
newsitem.headline: Shelling after Congo's Lissouba returns home.

text.p: President Pascal Lissouba, who left Congo on Monday for the first time since a civil war broke out three weeks ago, returned home to a fresh burst of fighting.

Mortar and machinegun fire rang out in the centre of the capital Brazzaville after dark, just an hour after Lissouba flew home from national day festivities across the river in Kinshasa in Laurent Kabila's "other" Congo.

"It seems to involve battles between bands of looters or soldiers letting off steam, rather than a threat or a deliberate break of the ceasefire by one side or the other," French ambassador Raymond Cesaire told Reuters by telephone.
Cesaire, the only foreign envoy left in the capital of Lissouba's oil-rich central African country, has kept his embassy open in the middle of the downtown no-man's land.
Brazzaville remained relatively calm earlier on Monday, the third day of a new ceasefire between Lissouba and his rival, former military leader Denis Sassou Nguesso.
The former colonial city, wartime capital for "Free French" leader General Charles de Gaulle, has been devastated by shelling, street battles and looting since June 5.
Aid workers estimate some 1,000 to 3,000 people, mostly civilians, have died in a conflict that has wavered between merciless artillery duels and truces that bring only relative and partial calm.
Some of the heaviest fighting has been for the city airport which seemed still to be firmly under Lissouba's control after he used it to fly to and from Kinshasa.
A lasting political solution for Congo seems no nearer.
Both Lissouba and Sassou say they want free and fair presidential elections, but disagree on how to hold them.
Sassou's Radio Congo Freedom said planeloads of Serb, Liberian and Angolan opposition UNITA mercenaries were flooding into the country to help Lissouba.

International mediation efforts led by Omar Bongo, president of neighbouring Gabon, have centered on the dispatch of an African intervention force but the United Nations says there must be a lasting peace first.
